Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Gaza Trump’s Gaza Board of Peace issues first building contract – for a military base Exclusive: Louisiana firm awarded tender to build rudimentary outpost to house Moroccan troops Aram Roston in Washington Thu 6 Aug 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 08.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, which was set up in January to oversee the reconstruction of Gaza , has finally issued its first construction contract in the devastated territory: a project to build a rudimentary 150-person military outpost to house Moroccan troops, a source familiar with the matter told the Guardian. The contract, which has not yet been finalised, was awarded to Arkel International, a Louisiana-based firm that has previously carried out work with the US government in countries such as Iraq. The Board of Peace is chaired by the US president and led by a team that includes his son-in-law Jared Kushner and friend Steve Witkoff. In an email, a Board of Peace official said the board and a group of Palestinian technocrats installed to oversee Gaza “are in the final stages of preparing several contract awards. None have been finalised.” The Palestinian group is known as the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza . The official said “one prospective contract concerns facilities to support the international stabilisation force (ISF), which will assist in implementing the roadmap’s security and governance arrangements”. They added: “This contract will be one of many that are essential for the future of Gaza .” Trump’s Board of Peace plans to grant itself sweeping immunity, documents show Read more The award comes just days after Trump announced that Hamas had agreed to disarm, though there are considerable questions about how the group would give up its guns. Israel has opposed the plan, and increased airstrikes in Gaza after Trump’s announcement . The Guardian reported in July that the board’s original Gaza reconstruction had shrunk dramatically from an ambitious blueprint to rebuild the whole territory to a small pilot project in the south of the strip. The base now being planned is just 100 metres by 120 metres and is intended to house a contingent of Moroccan troops, who would rotate from a base in Israel, the source said. It would lie in the 60% of Gaza’s territory that the Israeli army directly controls. Israeli forces have also created a buffer zone beyond that area. The source said the base was about a mile from the Israeli border and would have a “quick extraction route” in case the small force came under attack. View image in fullscreen Donald Trump’s original grandiose vision of a reconstructed Gaza is displayed by the president at the World Economic Forum meeting at Davos on 22 January. The UN resolution authorising the Board of Peace had approved establishing an “international stabilisation force” for Gaza, and there have been varying reports on which country would provide these troops. Morocco has promised a small contingent, but the legal framework for the ISF has yet to be finalised, and it is not clear when the deployment would begin. In earlier contract plans seen by the Guardian, the 150-person base was the first phase of a plan to build a 5,000-person military base in Gaza for the ISF . This base would have included “vehicle fighting positions” and a perimeter berm – or raised defensive bank – and would have rudimentary facilities suitable for short-term deployments. The earlier contract said the first phase would consist of “tents and cots for forces to sleep, as well as chemical toilets and handwashing stations. At this phase, this is what we would consider habitable.” Trump announced in February 2025 that the US would “take over” and “own” Gaza, although the agreement that set up the Board of Peace fell short of that. At the board’s first meeting in January, Kushner unveiled a “master plan” to build “New Gaza” with an expansive waterfront city with gleaming mixed-use towers. “It could be a hope, it could be a destination. A lot of industry,” he said. At least 80% of Gaza’s buildings were damaged or destroyed in the war. Ten months after the ceasefire, most of the territory’s 2 million people are still living in makeshift and unsanitary camps. Jul 25, 2026 4:57pm UTC Charles Leclerc has admitted that his pace “was never to the level” of Ferrari team mate Lewis Hamilton across Saturday’s Qualifying session for the Hungarian Grand Prix, with the Monegasque left to rue deficits in two key corners. Leclerc , who claimed pole at the Hungaroring in 2025, posted a fastest time of 1m 17.445s during the decisive Q3 phase, comparing to a 1m 17.219s from Hamilton and a 1m 17.207s from pole-sitting McLaren driver Lando Norris . Sharing his emotions after the session, Leclerc sighed: “I’m a bit disappointed. Disappointed mostly because I didn’t find a solution for Turn 1 and Turn 12 all today, really. “In FP3 already I was struggling with Turn 1 and Turn 12, and I was still losing three-tenths or something like this in Q3 in Turn 1 and Turn 12. I’m a bit disappointed with it. I’ll look into it to try and fix that for tomorrow.” Leclerc was outpaced by team mate Hamilton during Qualifying in Hungary He added: “Today there was quite a bit of a wind change, and I don’t think I did a great job anticipating it with the car set-up. I felt a little bit off from this morning, then Qualifying has been quite messy, to be honest. “We’ve been a bit unlucky in Q2 with the yellow flag in the last sector, then we were kind of trying to… We were playing catch-up. But the pace was never to the level of Lewis, so it was all about trying to maximise today. I felt I kind of did it.” Turning his attention to Sunday’s Grand Prix – which he will nonetheless start ahead of Hamilton, who was given a three-place grid penalty post-Qualifying for impeding Oscar Piastri – Leclerc pointed to the importance of nailing the long run down to Turn 1, with overtaking opportunities at a premium around the tight, twisty Budapest venue. “We were competitive all weekend,” he commented. “It’s true that today everybody seems to have done a big, big step forward that we didn’t do, but it’s still a long race tomorrow. “I do believe that our race pace is strong, but it’s true again that people have done a step forward since yesterday, so I’m pretty sure it’s going to be very close. On a track like this, the start particularly will be very key.” F1 Store - Ferrari Check out the latest Ferrari products in the F1 Store. https://www.dailyrecord.co.uk/news/scott.text: Jim Dowson’s extreme brand of conservatism has led to claims that he is the most influential far right figure in the UK. In 1999, Dowson made it clear that he would go to extreme lengths to make his ultra-conservative views stick in a changing world. His Precious Life Scotland anti abortion group shocked Scotland by using pictures of aborted foetuses in its campaigning. Dowson had already been involved with hard-line loyalist groups in the west of Scotland and the Catholic Church in Scotland moved to distance itself from anything he was a part of. At the same time he was reported to have been the organiser of a flute band in Cumbernauld, which recorded a tape in honour of Ulster Freedom Fighter murderer Michael Stone. Stone was jailed for attacking a Republican funeral in west Belfast, throwing hand grenades and firing at the mourners, including women and children. Three people were killed. After Dowson’s past came to light in the press, he admitted to having “a very murky past”. He said he had turned to Christianity - but that served only to harden his intolerant views. In 2012 the Daily Record told how Dowson had become the British National Party’s top fundraiser, closely aligned with leader Nick Griffin. He was forced out of his local Orange Lodge and took part in demonstrations against fellow Orangemen, attacking them as “atheists and boozers” after he was “born again”. For a time, Dowson began to shrink back from publicity, to the extent that The Times dubbed him “the invisible man of Britain’s far right”. All the time he was honing his knowledge and skills as a moneymaker - seeking out new markets, where racial tensions would lead to supporters reaching into their pockets with donations. The internet enabled him to look to the USA, where the pageantry and twisted history of the Knights Templar brought opportunities for sales. He helped found and worked as the main source of funding for Britain First, another far right group, from which he resigned in 2014. He became the front of the anti-immigrant Knights Templar International organisation, which led him to seek foreign shores for opportunity - both to raise cash and spread his views. A vocal supported of Donald Trump’s 2016 election campaign, Dowson connected to the hard right of the Republican movement, who were ripe for the scaremongering material he was circulating about the replacement of white societies. Dowson worked with anti-abortionists in the States to further his links there. Dowson’s public profile was enhanced with his Templar Report online, which has Nick Griffin as a regular guest. After setting up home in Northern Ireland, Dowson came to public notice in the Belfast City Hall flag protests that broke out in late 2012. That protest erupted after the city council voted to only fly the Union Flag from Belfast City Hall on seventeen designated days a year rather than constantly had previously. Dowson was charged with encouraging or assisting offenders and five counts of taking part in an unnotified public procession. In court he dressed in Islamic-style clothing and was given a three-month suspended sentence. In 2016, the Daily Record revealed that Dowson was spearheading a military group who hunted down asylum seekers in Bulgaria. Dowson donned camouflage fatigues to join the heavily armed Shipka Bulgarian National Movement, stalking migrants who cross the Turkish border. True to form, he was producing videos begging donors in Europe and America to send funds to arm the militia. Dowson appeared on Russian TV to promote the Knights Templar International - and whip up support for far-right groups in Hungary and other eastern states. Also true to form, Dowson was peddling a stilted culture war, claiming that the Turkey-Bulgaria border was the key strategic point to be defended from refugee “invaders” of Europe, who were, in his view, seeking to take over the world. By this stage, Dowson was well aware of the allure of militia gear for angry and misguided groups who fall under the far right spell. He boasted of supplying bulletproof vests, night vision goggles, drones and other supplies - and asking US supporters to sign up or send money. In a video from 2016, Dowson stated the same silver-tongued, divisive rhetoric that he regurgitated in Glasgow recently, spouting: “Today, the Knights Templar International brought along vests and ballistics and drones and night vision, stuff that these guys desperately need.” “A big thank you to supporters in America and the Philippines and other countries who have contributed to this. “These are men and women, mainly ex-forces, doing it in their own free time, facing all sorts of risks and dangers. These are good people and they’re very, very deserving of your support.” In another video, shameless Dowson tells the Bulgarian militia: “When my grandfather was alive, this land was ruled by Ottomans, by the Muslims. Now they’re coming back. Remember the forces of Islam once got as far as Vienna. Now they are as far as John O’Groats in Scotland and more and more are coming in. “This is not political, this is a fight between good and evil, black and white, a fight of the cross, a fight of Christ.” Earlier that year, Dowson and BNP supremo Nick Griffin travelled to St Petersburg in Russia for a rally of far-right groups. In May 2017, it was reported by Hope not Hate that Dowson had been stopped from entering Hungary after the Hungarian Immigration Authority declared him an “undesirable individual” and barred him from entering the country in future. Whilst attending a far-right conference in Budapest in March 2017, Dowson stated “England is stuffed, England is stuffed totally” and advanced his belief that an independent Scotland “would protect us from the excesses of Muslim domination”. Despite his strong bonds with extreme Loyalist groups, Dowson has carefully sought to nurture links with conservative Catholic supporters. He has been heavily associated with the Irish Catholic nationalist group Síol na hÉireann (Seed of Ireland). In recent months, Dowson has been a regular guest of convicted UVF bomber mark Sinclair - Freedom Dad - who has explicitly tried to link up the far right rabble rousers in Belfast to groups on Glasgow.
